title: Heat Transfer: Conduction, Convection and Radiation

questions.stem: Which kind of heat transfer is it? Sort the examples.
items: a metal pan handle gets hot
feet feel cold on a tiled floor
warm air rises from a heater
you feel warm in front of a fire
questions.explanation: Conduction passes heat through solids by touch. Convection is warm air or liquid rising. Radiation is heat travelling as invisible infrared rays, even through space.

questions.stem: Sort these materials into good conductors and good insulators of heat.
questions.explanation: Metals let heat through easily. Wool, wood and especially trapped air slow the flow of heat.

questions.stem: Heat from the Sun reaches the Earth through empty space. How does it travel?
questions.explanation: Radiation does not need particles, so infrared rays can cross empty space. Conduction and convection need particles.

questions.stem: In a solid, heat passes from particle to particle by ___. In liquids and gases, warm parts rise in a loop called ___.
questions.explanation: Conduction needs touching particles in a solid. Convection is the loop of rising warm and sinking cool fluid.

questions.stem: A big bucket of warm water holds more heat than a small cup of boiling water.
questions.explanation: Temperature tells us how hot something is, but heat depends on how much material there is as well. The bucket has many more particles holding energy.

questions.stem: Trapped air is a good insulator, which is why a woollen jumper keeps you warm.
questions.explanation: Wool traps many tiny pockets of air. Trapped air slows the movement of heat away from your body.

questions.stem: Explain, using particles, why a metal spoon in hot dal gets hot all the way up to the handle.
questions.model_answer: The particles at the hot end vibrate faster and bump into their neighbours, passing energy along the metal to the handle. This is conduction, and metal is a good conductor.
questions.explanation: In a solid the particles are close together, so hotter, faster-vibrating particles quickly pass energy to their neighbours.

questions.stem: Which parts of a vacuum flask slow down heat transfer? Choose all that are right.
options: a thin metal base touching the table
questions.explanation: The vacuum has no particles, so no conduction or convection. Shiny walls reflect radiation. The stopper stops warm air escaping by convection.

questions.stem: Put the steps in order to show how a convection current forms in a pot of water on a stove.
sequence: The stove heats the water at the bottom.
The warm water expands and becomes less dense.
Cooler, denser water sinks to take its place.
A loop of moving water forms: a convection current.
questions.explanation: Warm liquid is less dense and rises, and cooler, denser liquid sinks. The moving loop stirs the whole pot.

questions.stem: Match each key word to its meaning.
pairs: heat passing through a solid, particle to particle
heat carried by a moving liquid or gas
questions.explanation: These five words describe how heat moves and how materials handle it.

questions.stem: In which direction does heat move?
options: from hotter things to colder things
from colder things to hotter things
questions.explanation: Heat is energy that moves because of a temperature difference, from hot to cold, until the temperatures are the same.

questions.stem: A cook’s pan has a copper base and a plastic handle. Explain both choices.
questions.model_answer: Copper is a good conductor, so it passes heat quickly to the food. Plastic is an insulator, so the handle stays cool to hold.
questions.explanation: Pans need heat to flow into the food, so the base is a conductor. The handle must slow heat flow, so it is an insulator.

questions.stem: Look at the three pictures. Match each letter to the way heat travels.
questions.image_alt: Three pictures lettered A, B and C: a spoon in a hot drink, a pot of water over a flame with arrows, and the Sun warming a hand.
questions.explanation: A: a spoon in a hot drink gets hot by conduction. B: water moves in a loop over the flame (convection). C: the Sun warms a hand by radiation.

questions.stem: In picture B, why does the warm water at the bottom of the pot rise?
questions.image_alt: Three pictures lettered A, B and C: a spoon in a hot drink, a pot of water over a flame with arrows, and the Sun warming a hand.
options: It becomes heavier than the cool water.
It is pushed up by the spoon.
It expands and becomes less dense.
questions.explanation: Warm water expands, so it is less dense than the cooler water around it and floats upwards. Cooler, denser water sinks to take its place.

questions.stem: In the vacuum flask, which number is the **vacuum**, the empty space between the walls?
questions.image_alt: A vacuum flask cut in half with parts numbered 1 to 5.
questions.explanation: Number 3 is the vacuum. It has no particles, so heat cannot cross it by conduction or convection.

questions.stem: Which part of the flask reflects heat radiation back towards the hot drink?
questions.image_alt: A vacuum flask cut in half with parts numbered 1 to 5.
questions.explanation: Shiny surfaces reflect radiation, so the silver walls (2) send heat back instead of letting it escape. The stopper (1) stops warm air rising out.

questions.stem: Four cups hold the same hot water. Which cup will cool down the fastest?
questions.image_alt: Four cups of hot water: no cover, newspaper, wool and foil.
questions.explanation: Without a cover there is nothing to slow the heat loss. Newspaper and wool are insulators, and foil reflects radiation.

questions.stem: Where should a room heater be placed to warm the whole room best?
questions.explanation: Warm air rises, so a low heater sets up a convection current: warm air goes up and cooler air sinks to be warmed.

questions.stem: It is a very sunny day in Dhaka. Which shirt will keep Rafi coolest?
questions.explanation: Light colours reflect more of the Sun’s radiation and absorb less heat, so they stay cooler than dark clothes.

questions.stem: Mina wants her rice to stay warm for four hours on a school trip. Which is the best choice?
options: a tightly closed container wrapped in a woollen cloth
a metal tin with its lid off
a bowl placed on a cold stone
questions.explanation: A lid stops warm air escaping by convection, and wool is an insulator that slows conduction. An open metal bowl loses heat quickly.

questions.stem: Many homes in Dhaka have thin tin roofs that get very hot in the sun. Which ideas would help cool the room below? Choose all that are right.
options: add a jute or bamboo ceiling with an air gap
grow creepers or trees for shade
questions.explanation: White paint reflects radiation, jute and trapped air are insulators, and shade blocks the Sun. A black roof absorbs more heat, and removing a ceiling removes insulation.

questions.stem: Before lifting a hot metal pan from the stove, Sumi should use a cloth or oven glove, because metal conducts heat quickly.
questions.explanation: Metal is a good conductor, so a hot pan handle can burn bare hands. Cloth is an insulator and protects the skin.

questions.stem: In the simulation, the thermometer reading goes up while the burner heats the water.

sim.task: Open Energy Forms and Changes and choose the Intro screen. Put the beaker of water over a burner, slide the burner to heat, and watch the thermometer.

questions.explanation: Heat from the burner makes the water particles move faster, so the temperature rises.

questions.stem: In the simulation, a hot iron block touches a cooler brick block. What happens to their temperatures?

sim.task: Open Energy Forms and Changes and choose the Intro screen. Heat the iron block with a burner, then move it so that it touches the cooler brick block. Watch both thermometers.

options: The iron cools down and the brick warms up.
The iron gets hotter and the brick colder.
The brick cools down and the iron warms up.
questions.explanation: Heat flows from the hotter object to the colder one by conduction, until they reach about the same temperature.

questions.stem: In the simulation, when the burner is slid to the cooling side under the water, the thermometer reading goes down.

sim.task: Open Energy Forms and Changes and choose the Intro screen. Slide the burner under the beaker of water to the cooling side and watch the thermometer.

questions.explanation: Cooling takes heat energy out of the water, so its particles slow down and the temperature falls.

questions.stem: Class 5B wrapped three cans of water in black paper, white paper and shiny foil and put them in the sun (example data). After 40 minutes: black 45 °C, white 35 °C, foil 32 °C, all starting at 28 °C. The black can ended ___ °C hotter than the foil can.
questions.explanation: 45 − 32 = 13 °C. Dark, dull surfaces absorb radiation best, and shiny foil reflects most of it.

questions.stem: Use the can results (start 28 °C; after 40 minutes black 45 °C, white 35 °C, foil 32 °C). Which conclusions are supported? Choose all that are right.
options: The black can warmed the most.
The shiny foil can warmed the least.
The white can warmed faster than the black can.
Dark colours would keep a can cooler in the sun.
The white can rose by 7 °C in 40 minutes.
questions.explanation: Black rose 17 °C, white 7 °C and foil 4 °C. Dark colours absorb more radiation, so they heat up faster, not stay cooler.

questions.stem: A community group measured four rooms at 2 pm (example data): bare tin roof 41 °C, white-painted roof 36 °C, jute ceiling with air gap 35 °C, tree shade + white roof 32 °C. How much cooler was the best room than the bare tin roof room?
questions.explanation: 41 − 32 = 9 °C. The shade stops radiation reaching the roof and the white paint reflects the rest.

questions.stem: Design a lunch box that keeps rice hot for four hours. Say how it reduces conduction, convection **and** radiation.
questions.model_answer: Double walls with an air gap or a wool cover reduce conduction. A tight lid stops warm air escaping, which reduces convection. A shiny inner lining reflects radiation.
questions.explanation: Each part tackles one kind of heat transfer: insulators slow conduction, a lid stops convection and shiny surfaces reflect radiation, just like a vacuum flask.

questions.stem: Which statement about heat and temperature is correct?
options: Hot things always hold more heat than cooler things.
Temperature and heat are two names for the same thing.
A thermometer measures how much heat an object holds.
A bucket of warm water holds more heat than a cup of boiling water.
questions.explanation: Temperature is how hot something is. Heat depends on temperature and on how much material there is, so a large bucket can hold more heat than a small cup.
